title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 19
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A supermarket introduced an own-brand range priced below the branded equivalents and reports that its total profit rose. It concludes that customers switching to own-brand products are more profitable for the chain.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Own-brand products are manufactured by the same firms that make the branded ones.
B. Own-brand packaging is cheaper to produce.
C. Branded suppliers responded by increasing the payments they make for shelf space, and that increase accounts for most of the profit rise.
D. Some customers buy both ranges.
E. The range was introduced in stages.
questions.explanation: The profit rise is traced to a different source, so it supports no conclusion about the margin on switched purchases.

questions.prompt: A care home group reports that homes with the highest staff-to-resident ratios receive the best inspection ratings, and proposes raising ratios across all its homes to improve ratings.
questions.question: The proposal assumes which of the following?
options: A. Inspectors weight staffing more heavily than other criteria.
B. The rating difference reflects staffing levels rather than other features of the better-staffed homes.
C. Additional staff can be recruited at current wages.
D. Residents prefer homes with more staff.
E. Inspections are conducted annually.
questions.explanation: Better-funded homes may have both more staff and better everything else; the proposal needs staffing to be doing the work. C is a feasibility condition rather than a premise of the inference.

questions.prompt: A surveying firm replaced ground crews with drones and reports that it now completes twice as many site surveys per week. It concludes that drones have doubled its productivity.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How much the drones cost to purchase
B. Whether clients prefer drone surveys
C. How many staff the firm employs
D. Whether the drone surveys require ground verification that the firm counts separately
E. Whether drones can operate in high winds
questions.explanation: If part of the work has been moved outside the counted unit, surveys per week overstates the change in total output per hour.

questions.prompt: A study found that people who wear fitness trackers walk more than people who do not, and a newspaper reports that wearing a tracker increases physical activity.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the newspaper's report?
options: A. Trackers vary in accuracy.
B. Some owners stop wearing their trackers after a few months.
C. Trackers also measure sleep.
D. Walking is only one form of exercise.
E. People buy trackers when they have already decided to become more active, and activity in tracker owners was already rising before purchase.
questions.explanation: Pre-purchase trends show the direction of causation running the other way; C would attenuate a real effect rather than explain the association away.

questions.prompt: Every route in the Danesford bus network that runs after nine in the evening is operated with low-floor vehicles. No route operated with low-floor vehicles has been reduced in frequency this year. Some routes in the network have been reduced in frequency this year.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some routes in the network do not run after nine in the evening.
B. Low-floor vehicles are more reliable.
C. Most routes run after nine in the evening.
D. No evening route will ever be reduced.
E. Reduced routes carry fewer passengers.
questions.explanation: Reduced routes are not operated with low-floor vehicles, and evening running implies those vehicles, so the reduced routes do not run after nine. B and E introduce claims the statements do not support.

questions.prompt: A dealer notes that used cars with full service histories sell for more than those without, and advises owners to keep their service records in order to increase the value of their cars.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the advice as a general recommendation?
options: A. Service histories can be reconstructed from garage records.
B. Some buyers do not ask to see the history.
C. Cars with full histories are those whose owners maintained them properly, and the price difference reflects the condition of the vehicle rather than the paperwork.
D. Dealers charge a fee for verifying histories.
E. Electric cars require less servicing.
questions.explanation: If the paperwork marks maintenance rather than creating value, keeping records without maintaining the car will not produce the premium.

questions.prompt: A government reports that farm incomes rose in the years after it introduced a subsidy for arable production, and concludes that the subsidy raised farm incomes.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. World grain prices doubled over the same period, and incomes rose as much on farms ineligible for the subsidy.
B. The subsidy was paid annually.
C. Some farmers did not apply for the subsidy.
D. Administration of the scheme was expensive.
E. Livestock farms were excluded from the scheme.
questions.explanation: An ineligible comparison group showing the same rise attributes the change to prices rather than to the subsidy.

questions.prompt: A library extended its opening hours and reports that the number of items borrowed rose. The council concludes that longer opening hours increase reading.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the cost of employing additional staff
B. does not distinguish between adult and children's books
C. relies on data from a single library
D. overlooks electronic lending
E. treats items borrowed as a measure of reading
questions.explanation: Borrowing is a transaction; it may rise because the same readers visit at more convenient times without anyone reading more.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer of sports drinks cites a study in which athletes performed better after consuming its product than after consuming water, and advertises the drink as improving athletic performance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement?
options: A. The study was conducted at high altitude.
B. The athletes knew which drink they were receiving, and a later study in which the drinks were disguised found no difference.
C. The drink contains sugar.
D. Some athletes prefer the taste of water.
E. The study measured endurance rather than speed.
questions.explanation: A blinded replication finding nothing is close to decisive against an unblinded original, since it removes the expectation the first design left in.

questions.prompt: A factory installed equipment to sort its waste for recycling and reports that the proportion of its waste sent to landfill fell from 60 per cent to 25 per cent. Management describes this as a substantial environmental improvement.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the description?
options: A. The equipment was expensive to install.
B. Some sorted material is exported for processing.
C. Staff required training to use the equipment.
D. The factory's total waste doubled over the same period, so the absolute quantity sent to landfill rose.
E. Landfill charges have increased.
questions.explanation: A falling proportion of a growing total can mean more landfill, not less; the claim was about environmental effect rather than about the ratio.

questions.prompt: A mobile network offers customers a discount for signing a two-year contract rather than a one-year contract, and reports that two-year customers are more satisfied with the service. It concludes that longer contracts improve customer satisfaction.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the conclusion?
options: A. Two-year contracts cost less per month.
B. Satisfaction is measured by an annual survey.

C. Customers who expect to be satisfied with the network are the ones willing to commit for two years, and dissatisfied customers on one-year contracts are counted while dissatisfied two-year customers have not yet reached renewal.
D. The network covers most of the country.
E. Some customers switch networks when their contract ends.
questions.explanation: Two selection effects run the same way: who chooses the long contract, and who has had the opportunity to leave. Neither requires the contract length to do anything.

questions.passageText:
A warranty is usually described as insurance: the buyer is protected against the cost of failure. That account is incomplete, and in some markets it is the least important of the functions a warranty performs.

Consider the buyer's problem before purchase. Two machines look alike and the buyer cannot tell which is more reliable. A manufacturer confident of its product can offer a long warranty cheaply, because few claims will be made; a manufacturer whose product fails often cannot match the offer without incurring costs it cannot bear. The warranty therefore separates the two, and it does so whether or not any buyer ever makes a claim. Its informational function is discharged at the moment of sale.

This explains an otherwise puzzling pattern. Warranties are longest in categories where buyers cannot inspect quality and failures are expensive, and they are often shortest where a product's reliability is easily observed or where users can be blamed for damage. It also explains why extending a warranty is a common competitive response to a reputation problem: the firm is making a costly statement rather than offering a service.

The complication is that warranties also change buyer behaviour. A covered buyer takes less care, and manufacturers respond with the exclusions and conditions that make warranty documents what they are. Those clauses are frequently read as evasions, and some are; but a warranty with no conditions at all would be an insurance policy against carelessness, and priced accordingly.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that a warranty's informational function is discharged
options: A. when a claim is made
B. at the end of the warranty period
C. when the manufacturer publishes failure rates
D. only if the buyer reads the conditions
E. at the moment of sale
questions.explanation: The separating function operates whether or not any buyer ever claims.

questions.passageText:
Commercial programmes promising general cognitive improvement rest on a claim that is testable and has been tested extensively: that practice on a computerised task improves not only that task but abilities used elsewhere.

The first part is not in doubt. People who practise a working-memory task get better at it, sometimes dramatically. The disputed part is transfer, and here the evidence has settled into a pattern. Near transfer — improvement on tasks closely resembling the trained one — is regularly observed. Far transfer to unrelated abilities, such as reasoning or academic attainment, is small, inconsistent, and largest in the studies with the weakest controls.

That last regularity is the informative one. Trials comparing training against a passive control, in which the comparison group does nothing, report larger effects than trials using an active control, in which the comparison group performs a different demanding activity. The difference implicates expectation: participants who know they have been given a treatment described as improving cognition perform better on tests administered by the people who told them so.

The reasonable summary is not that cognitive training is worthless. Practice does produce durable skill on the practised task, which may be worth having, and specific programmes for specific deficits have shown targeted benefits. What has not been shown is the marketed claim: that a general capacity can be raised by exercising it, in the way a muscle is strengthened by lifting. The muscle analogy is doing more persuasive work in the advertising than any finding does.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that improvement on the trained task itself is
options: A. disputed
B. observed only with active controls
C. smaller than far transfer
D. not in doubt
E. confined to young adults
questions.explanation: The first sentence of the second paragraph states this, and the dispute is located at transfer.

questions.passageTitle: Trade and the Places That Lost
questions.passageText:
That trade raises aggregate income is among the better-supported propositions in economics. That its costs fall on identifiable places and workers, and persist there far longer than the standard model implied, is a more recent finding and has changed the debate.

The older account acknowledged that some workers lose while consumers gain, but assumed adjustment: displaced workers would move to other industries or regions, and the loss would be temporary. Studies tracking local labour markets exposed to rapid import competition found otherwise. Employment fell and did not recover; wages fell for those who remained; and the effects spread beyond the directly affected industries into local services, because a shock to a place's largest employer is a shock to everything that employer's wages supported.

Mobility turned out to be the weak assumption. Workers moved less than the model expected, for reasons that are not mysterious: housing, family, the cost of retraining, and the fact that a house in a declining region is worth least exactly when its owner needs to sell it.

None of this reverses the aggregate case, and the policy conclusion drawn by some — that the trade should not have occurred — does not follow from evidence about how its costs were distributed. What does follow is that compensation which exists only in theory is not compensation, and that a policy justified by gains sufficient to offset losses acquires an obligation to arrange the offsetting rather than to note that it would be possible.
questions.prompt: The older account of trade adjustment assumed that
options: A. displaced workers would move to other industries or regions, making the loss temporary
B. no workers would be displaced
C. consumers would not benefit
D. wages would rise in affected regions
E. local services would be unaffected
questions.explanation: The passage identifies mobility as the weak assumption in that account.

options: A. service firms also faced imports
B. workers retrained into service occupations

questions.passageText:
English spelling was variable for centuries, and its stabilisation was not the discovery of correct forms but the outcome of decisions by printers, schoolmasters and dictionary-makers whose reasons were often incidental to the language.

Printing did much of the work. A compositor setting type needed forms he could set quickly, and the practice of justifying a line by adding or removing a final letter shows how far convenience shaped what became standard. Early printers were sometimes foreign, and forms from their own orthographies entered English by that route. Some of the oddities that pupils are now taught as rules originated as such accidents, or as deliberate learned interventions — the silent letter inserted to display a word's Latin ancestry, sometimes a mistaken ancestry.

Dictionaries then fixed what printing had made common. A lexicographer choosing between two current forms was making a decision that would be quoted back as authority, and the eighteenth-century dictionaries acquired that status quickly because they satisfied a demand for a standard rather than because their choices were better argued than the alternatives.

The result is a system whose irregularities are historical residue rather than design, and whose defenders sometimes describe as etymologically informative what is more accurately described as inherited. That is not an argument for reform, which has its own difficulties, but it is a reason to be careful about treating the current spelling of a word as evidence of anything except which forms happened to be common when the fixing occurred.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the practice of justifying a line of type
options: A. required printers to standardise spelling nationally
B. was abandoned in the eighteenth century
C. shows how far convenience shaped forms that became standard
D. originated with foreign compositors
E. had no effect on spelling
questions.explanation: Adding or removing a final letter to fit a line is given as the illustration of incidental influence.
